Portfolio Optimization
Under Estimation Error.

Efficient frontiers, robust covariance estimation and out-of-sample portfolio construction.

What looks optimal when estimated from history? How much of that answer survives uncertain inputs, concentration, trading and a strictly chronological test?

01 / Research question

How much should we trust an optimized portfolio?

Mean–variance optimization can produce precise weights from imprecise historical estimates. This study asks whether allocations based on estimated returns and covariance stay useful after resampling uncertainty and live-like re-estimation.

Observed trade-off

Constraints helped more than covariance shrinkage

On the 2013-01-07–2026-09-25 walk-forward sample, the uncapped sample maximum-Sharpe portfolio has net Sharpe 0.55 and mean effective positions 2.27. A 25% position cap raises those to 0.64 and 4.40 while cutting annual turnover from 2.95 to 1.36.

Practical benchmark

The evidence is mixed

On the rolling 2013-01-07–2026-09-25 test, equal weighting earns 6.3% compounded annually with Sharpe 0.50; the capped optimizer earns 7.0% and Sharpe 0.64. Yet the one-time 2019-01-02–2026-09-25 holdout reverses this: fixed equal weight earns 9.3% against 5.4% for the fixed capped optimizer. Both comparisons matter.

The in-sample question is “which weights maximize an estimated objective?” The investable question is “which decisions remain defensible when estimates and markets change?”

02 / Asset universe & data

Ten diversified ETFs, one fixed universe.

U.S.-listed asset-class ETFs provide a common adjusted-price history from 2010-01-04 to 2026-09-25. BIL is downloaded separately as a short-Treasury ETF cash proxy and is never optimized as a risky asset. Issuer inception dates predate the selected 2010 start. Each symbol has 4,208 aligned prices and no missing adjusted close in this chosen period; the common panel loses 0 provider calendar rows. Median daily share volume exceeds the 500,000-share screen for every symbol, but this does not prove that every trade could be executed at the reported close.

03 / Portfolio framework

Clear conventions before optimization.

All calculations use daily arithmetic simple returns, Rₜ = Pₜ / Pₜ₋₁ − 1, from positive distribution-adjusted prices. Portfolio return is the weighted sum of constituent simple returns. Daily log returns add through time for a single asset; they are not silently substituted into this portfolio's linear return and covariance formulas. Reported annual compounded returns are geometric wealth growth, distinct from annualized arithmetic sample means.

Portfolio model
E[Rₚ] = wᵀμ   |   σₚ² = wᵀΣw   |   σₚ = √(wᵀΣw)
Σᵢ wᵢ = 1   |   wᵢ ≥ 0   |   capped cases: wᵢ ≤ 0.25

μ is the vector of estimated annual arithmetic returns, Σ the annualized daily covariance matrix, and w invested capital weights. Covariance determines how assets move together, so portfolio volatility is not a weighted average of standalone volatilities. Daily means and covariances are multiplied by 252; volatility scales by √252. These are finite-sample estimates, not population parameters.

Objectives
Equal weight: wᵢ = 1/N
GMV: min wᵀΣ̂w
Estimated maximum Sharpe: max (wᵀμ̂ − r̂f) / √(wᵀΣ̂w)
Efficient frontier: min wᵀΣ̂w subject to wᵀμ̂ = μtarget

The risk-free benchmark is the trailing arithmetic annualized return of BIL's adjusted prices, not an assumed constant. In the full training sample its estimate is 0.24%. BIL is an ETF with fees and price noise; its return is an imperfect proxy for a frictionless cash rate. Realized daily BIL returns are subtracted for reported out-of-sample Sharpe ratios.

04 / In-sample portfolios

Classical optimization prefers concentrated answers.

Using only the 2010-01-05–2018-12-31 window, the long-only GMV portfolio puts 89.9% in AGG and has 1.23 effective positions. Estimated maximum Sharpe puts 79.3% in AGG with 1.51 effective positions. The optimizer is responding to observed bond risk and return, not discovering a timeless economic law.

The table is deliberately labeled in-sample. Expected-return optimization looks attractive here, but its estimated Sharpe is conditional on noisy μ̂. A 25% ex-ante cap sacrifices some fitted Sharpe while materially reducing concentration. Equal weight is a real investable benchmark: it avoids parameter estimation, though it still rebalances and bears asset-class risk.

A separate chronological check

Weights fitted only through 2018-12-31 are then held as fixed targets from 2019-01-02 through 2026-09-25, restored monthly with the same 5 bp cost convention. No test return affects these target weights. This is a one-time holdout diagnostic; the later walk-forward analysis is the primary adaptive strategy test.

The fixed capped maximum-Sharpe portfolio does not travel well: its 5.4% CAGR and 0.33 Sharpe trail equal weight's 9.3% and 0.60. Over those same calendar dates, the rolling capped strategy reaches 9.5% and 0.67. Updating estimates helped in this realized period, but the two implementations differ in rebalance history and the fixed holdout pays an initial deployment cost.

05 / Efficient frontier

The frontier is an estimate, not a promise.

The curve is solved at feasible target arithmetic returns under full investment and long-only bounds. The curvature varies along the frontier: a broad middle section is nearly straight in these data, while the ends bend more visibly. Long-only bounds also change which assets have positive optimal weights as the target return rises, so this need not resemble a single unconstrained arc. Points below it have higher estimated volatility for a given estimated return. The sample maximum-Sharpe point uses the trailing BIL estimate as its reference rate. An asset manager should treat frontier geometry as a diagnostic of input assumptions: modest changes to mean estimates can move its tangent portfolio substantially. CVX Group's constrained portfolio formulation.

06 / Expected-return estimation error

Small input changes, large allocation changes.

The optimizer sees μ̂ and Σ̂, not population μ and Σ. The standard error of a historical mean shrinks slowly, particularly for volatile assets and correlated observations. To isolate mean dependence, 300 seeded experiments add independent normal shocks with standard deviation equal to half each asset's annualized training-mean standard error; the covariance estimate is held fixed.

The weight ranges make the sensitivity concrete. AGG's 5th–95th interval is 0%–87%; SPY's is 0%–49%. Boundary switches indicate that the fitted best asset mix is much less precise than its point estimate. These are local stress tests, not confidence intervals for true optimal weights; the independent-shock assumption ignores cross-asset estimation dependence.

07 / Resampling uncertainty

There is a distribution of “optimal” portfolios.

For each of 300 iid bootstrap draws, the pipeline resamples training dates, re-estimates both means and covariance, and re-solves long-only GMV and estimated maximum Sharpe. The random seed is fixed at 42. The resulting intervals describe estimator sensitivity conditional on the historical sample and resampling scheme.

AGG's GMV 5th–95th range is 89%–91%, far narrower than the maximum-Sharpe range. The latter changes as return rankings move under resampling. Even the steadier GMV result is economically concentrated in one bond fund; stability of a concentrated estimate does not remove model or regime risk. Iid resampling understates dependence and volatility clustering in financial returns.

08 / Shrinkage & constraints

Regularization has distinct jobs.

Ledoit–Wolf estimates daily covariance by shrinking the sample covariance toward a scaled-identity target, then annualizes it. Its fitted training shrinkage intensity is 0.55%. This is covariance regularization; it does not repair noisy historical expected returns. The 25% cap is a separate ex-ante decision limit. It prevents single-name dominance even when the fitted objective prefers it.

In this universe, shrinkage barely changes the training GMV weights. Out of sample, its GMV annual volatility is 4.8% versus 4.7% with sample covariance, while Sharpe is 0.32 versus 0.24. This is not strong evidence that shrinkage improves risk here; it modestly changes realized returns. Adding shrinkage to the capped maximum-Sharpe portfolio changes net Sharpe from 0.64 to 0.63, a negligible difference.

09 / Risk decomposition

Capital weights conceal risk concentration.

Euler volatility allocation
MRCᵢ = (Σw)ᵢ / σₚ   |   RCᵢ = wᵢMRCᵢ   |   ΣᵢRCᵢ = σₚ
HHI = Σᵢwᵢ²   |   N_eff = 1 / HHI

Equal weight has an effective count of 10 by construction. The training GMV count is 1.23, while the capped maximum-Sharpe count is 4.30. The code verifies that risk contributions add back to modeled portfolio volatility. A position cap controls capital concentration, yet correlated equity sleeves can still dominate risk. A risk manager needs both views.

10 / Walk-forward design

Every decision precedes its test return.

The primary test begins 2013-01-07 and ends 2026-09-25 (3,451 daily returns). On the first available session of each month, each strategy estimates 756 trailing daily observations ending before the rebalance date, chooses weights, and holds them until the next month. Six strategies isolate equal weighting, sample versus shrunk GMV, and sample versus shrunk maximum-Sharpe with and without a 25% position cap. No future return enters a training window.

The 2010–2018 chronological split above is an in-sample diagnostic; the rolling backtest is the main out-of-sample evaluation. Its early years overlap the fixed training period in calendar time, but every walk-forward prediction is still formed only from prior daily data. Portfolio weights drift with constituent returns between trades.

11 / Realized results

Optimization's out-of-sample gain is conditional.

GMV · sample2.7%4.7%0.24-15.4%0.251.25

In this sample, capped sample maximum Sharpe leads equal weight by 0.64 percentage points of annual compounded return and 0.13 in excess-return Sharpe, with lower realized volatility. Uncapped maximum Sharpe gives little additional return while increasing turnover and concentration. GMV lowers volatility sharply to 4.7%, but its 2.7% CAGR and 0.24 Sharpe trail equal weight. An investor targeting lower absolute risk might still prefer it; the objective is different.

Equal weighting is a serious comparison rather than a straw man. The capped optimizer's observed advantage depends on the selected ETF universe, 2013–2026 regimes, BIL proxy, and 5 bp cost model. It is not evidence of alpha or a reliable future Sharpe.

12 / Drawdown & risk forecasts

Predicted risk is not realized risk.

The walk-forward sample GMV strategy's mean predicted annual volatility is 4.2% and its realized volatility is 4.7%. For uncapped maximum Sharpe the same comparison is 8.4% predicted versus 10.3% realized. Averaging monthly risk forecasts is not itself a calibrated forecast test, but these gaps warn against treating fitted volatility as a guarantee. Drawdowns also show losses that a single variance estimate hides.

13 / Turnover & transaction costs

A fitted edge must pay for trading.

Cost convention
Turnoverₜ = Σᵢ |wᵢ,new − wᵢ,pretrade|
Costₜ = 0.0005 × Turnoverₜ
1 + Rnet,ₜ = (1 − Costₜ)(1 + Rgross,ₜ)

This is absolute traded notional, with no factor of one-half; a 100% switch from one asset to another counts 200% turnover. Pretrade weights include prior-day drift. The first deployment from cash is charged. At an illustrative 5 basis points per unit turnover, annual CAGR drag is 0.158 percentage points for uncapped maximum Sharpe, 0.073 for capped maximum Sharpe, and 0.019 for equal weight.

The measured cost drag is small relative to return uncertainty at this low assumed rate, but the turnover gap is material. Real execution depends on spreads, volume, market impact, taxes and rebalancing mechanics. These are neither broker quotes nor a claim of implementable net performance.

15 / Reliability & limits

Three different uncertainties.

Estimation error

Finite historical samples

Means are noisy, covariance shifts, and bootstrap intervals depend on iid resampling. Sample Sharpe ratios have substantial uncertainty. The study does not claim statistical significance for small differences.

Model error

Changing regimes

Mean–variance objectives compress downside asymmetry into two moments. ETF returns are not iid Gaussian; correlations can rise or reverse during stress. Product selection and surviving ETF histories also bias the historical universe. DBC's underlying index methodology changed in 2025, weakening a constant-exposure interpretation.

Implementation error

Data and trading

Yahoo adjusted closes can be revised or contain errors; distributions are provider-adjusted. BIL is not a frictionless bill rate. Flat turnover costs omit spreads, impact, taxes and exchange-specific execution.

The pipeline rejects duplicate dates, missing aligned returns, nonpositive adjusted prices, extreme one-day adjusted returns, asymmetric or non-PSD sample covariance, failed optimizations, infeasible bounds and any training window ending on or after its test date. These checks reduce coding risk but cannot validate future market relationships.

16 / Reproducibility & conclusion

What survives the audit?

Classical optimization gives a sharply concentrated in-sample answer: the sample GMV and maximum-Sharpe portfolios lean heavily on AGG. Bootstrap and mean perturbations show that maximum-Sharpe weights are much less dependable than a single output vector suggests. A 25% cap reduces concentration and turnover, and improved the observed rolling out-of-sample Sharpe here. Covariance shrinkage made only modest changes in this ten-ETF study. Equal weight stayed competitive and decisively beat every fixed optimized portfolio in the 2019-01-02–2026-09-25 chronological holdout.

The practical finding is conditional: monthly re-estimation plus a position cap helped on this realized path, whereas a single historical estimate did not travel well. The rolling advantage over equal weight is too small and design-sensitive to treat as a universal prescription. The next research step would test independent data sources and richer costs before exploring return-estimate shrinkage, Black–Litterman or robust optimization.

Reproduce locally

cd research/portfolio-optimization
python -m venv .venv
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pytest tests -q
python -m analysis.run_analysis

The analysis writes cached provider data, a cleaned return panel, auditable CSV/JSON results and SVG figures. The standalone HTML is generated from those executed results and can open without Python or a chart runtime. To redownload provider data, add --refresh; provider revisions can change the numerical results.
